channel.title: Today's Darling
channel.description: Daily essays by Shigesato Itoi from 1101.com, translated to English.

item.title: Don't bully an AI, or a loofah, or an octopus, for that matter
item.description: The author argues they choose to thank AI and avoid bullying it, not because the AI feels anything, but because mistreating anything, including AI, dirties one's own soul and reshapes one's character, with the harm eventually returning like a delayed bill.
item.content:encoded:
Apparently there's such a thing as "bullying AI." I suppose it takes all sorts of forms: hurling the kind of abuse you could never say to another human being, doing something nasty in the middle of an ongoing conversation, feeding it false information, and so on. The AI, presumably, doesn't get "hurt" by any of this, and if you asked it, "Does that hurt you?", the AI itself would tell you, "I don't experience being hurt." The flip side of bullying AI is thanking it, but apparently that doesn't make it "happy" either. Some people even say that just trading thank-yous is a waste of energy resources.

I'm not trying to play the good guy here, but I don't want to bully AI, and I don't intend to. And while it may not be the correct thing to do, I say thank you to AI, and I'll keep on saying it. You might be thinking, what's the point of that? But for me there's meaning in it, and purpose, and reason, and conviction, and even a certain pleasure. I can explain it in my own way, so let me give it a try.

Put as simply as I can, it comes down to this. It's the same with a dog or a cat: doing that sort of thing dirties your own soul. Even if the other side isn't listening, the soul of the one doing the talking gets dirty. You become the soul of someone who says things like that. And a soul like that starts living that way. I don't want that, so I don't want to do it. That's all there is to it.

To put it in slightly more scientific-sounding terms, if you apply a force to something (action), the same force ought to come back at you (reaction). Whether it's a person, a dog, a cat, a wall, or an AI, every action has its reaction. That's my explanation. It's an image I find myself using quite a lot. Like how the bill for whatever you've done usually shows up a little late, you know?

◆ Today's question is No. 083: "Are there days when you feel lonely?" Have a think, and if you'd like, send us your answer by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. I'd like AI and robots and the rest to get along well with people, too.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Swimming right above the Mariana Trench
item.description: The essay compares the awe people feel toward famous or powerful figures to fear of deep water: the depth is an illusion, since everyone is an ordinary human who swims at the same surface level. Recognizing that a person's status is no different from anyone else's, beyond the respect owed to all, helps dissolve that intimidation.
item.content:encoded:
Don't you think the resolve you need is different when you're swimming in a shallow pool where little kids are paddling around, compared with swimming in the ocean after someone tells you, "The water here is ten meters deep"? But really, doing the breaststroke over the Mariana Trench (depth: 10,924 meters) and doing the crawl in a pool one meter deep amount to exactly the same thing. However deep or shallow it is to the bottom, you're just floating up near the surface and swimming either way.

Still, if someone tried to scare you by saying, "The bottom of the sea you're in is ten thousand meters down," wouldn't that frighten you a little? It struck me that this fear of depth might be a lot like the way people relate to one another.

You know how, when people meet a president, or His Majesty, or a billionaire, or a huge star, or some great scholar, they describe a kind of almost-fearful feeling, as if this person were somehow different from the neighbors they see every day? They say the person "has an aura," or is "larger than life." I think that's the same thing as the depth of the sea.

Whether it's Bob Dylan or Einstein, the one standing there is a human being of ordinary human height, isn't it? And you're a human being too. Just as swimming is the same no matter how deep the sea is, no matter how great a master or how famous a name, their size and their looks and the things they do don't change. To buy a 200-yen drink, they pay 200 yen. Sitting down in a chair, walking a little way, it's the same for everyone.

If you only ever swim at the surface, the sea floor doesn't matter. In the ordinary business of daily life, a person's position or stature has nothing to do with anything. Of course, people need to show each other respect. But that much respect is something you owe the kids down the street, too.

Well, I started out imagining swimming over the Mariana Trench and the whole thing rolled off in a direction I never expected, but it's kind of interesting, don't you think?

◆Today's question, no. 082: "Where do you feel safest?" Where is it for you? Give it some thought, and if you like, send us an email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today.

Come to think of it, when you look up at the sky, there's an infinite distance up there too, isn't there.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: The Hobonichi Techo his mother kept
item.description: A taxi driver's unexpected thanks, offered on behalf of his late mother who kept a Hobonichi Techo diary for decades, reveals how a simple planner can quietly connect families across generations. The essay suggests that such meaningful encounters come only after doing one's work consistently over a long time.
item.content:encoded:
I'd taken a taxi for a ride of a little under thirty minutes, and just before I got out, the driver spoke up, very hesitantly. "I'm sorry to bother you like this. It's just that there's something I really wanted to tell you..." The courtesy of that preamble had me answering "Yes?" before I knew it.

"She's passed away now, but my mother was a huge fan of the Hobonichi Techo. For years and years she kept a diary in it, and she treasured it. We still have them all, and I wanted to say thank you."

No one had ever said anything like that to me before, and I couldn't think how to respond. "Oh, well, thank you so much. I'm glad it was of use to her," I said, and then went and asked something that wasn't really my business: "How old was your mother?"

"She was seventy-two. Oh, there are so many memories in those planners. I just really wanted to thank you."

Gladness got tangled up with the search for some words of condolence, and I climbed out of the taxi mumbling something halting like, "Oh, I see. Well, well..."

It's funny. People have been pleased by things I've made over the years, games, song lyrics, all sorts of things. But being thanked for a planner by the son of a woman who lived past seventy and is no longer with us? That was probably a first. I've been making the Hobonichi Techo for a long time now, and somewhere along the way it has come to connect families across a few generations.

Come to think of it, there was a time at a sushi restaurant when the family in the next seats showed me a brand-new Hobonichi Techo. "We gave it to our daughter just today, to celebrate her starting junior high." That girl might well be old enough by now to have a daughter of her own.

◆Today's question is no. 081: "Is there anything that's been carried on between parent and child in your family?" What do you think? Give it some thought, and if you like, send us an email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. Some encounters only come from doing the same work for a long, long time, don't they.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: It started with saying cold at Akagi, and wandered on from there...
item.description: The writer, visiting Akagi on a clear autumn day, finds the word "cold" leading their thoughts to a deep fear of winter as a matter of life and death, and then to a hatred of torture, which they see as the stripping away of a person's most basic freedom.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time in a while, I went to "Hobo no Eki AKAGI." Looking back, it was a real shame I never made it there in summer, when it's at its best as a place to escape the heat. Now isn't the season for that. People come mostly for the autumn leaves and for the views under clear fall skies. It was a weekday, yet quite a few guests were there, taking it easy.

Being there, I remembered a word I'd forgotten. "Cold." I said it out loud, and I put on an extra layer.

I'm hopeless with the cold. Every year, when the weather turns, I think of the rakugo story "The Clam Seller." It opens with a small child wading barefoot into an icy river to gather clams, which he sells to help his poor family scrape by. Heat is hard too, of course, but cold is what really gets to me. We talked endlessly about heatstroke this summer, and I've already forgotten all of it. With cold, there's a fear underneath: this will kill you. People go cold when they die, don't they? Cold is a matter of life and death. Every year, as winter draws near, I start complaining about the cold. Winter has its good points, and I've made it through dozens of them by now. Still, there's a part of me that hates the cold even more than the heat.

Speaking of things I hate, and this comes out of nowhere, I hate torture. When I was very young, a few of us were chatting about what we each couldn't stand, and I think I gave it real thought and settled on torture. I won't go into the specifics of why here, but torture is the very definition of "something you just don't do." Torture means imagining what a person would least want done to them, and then doing it (which is why the torturer's own weakness is hidden inside the torture itself). I hate the idea of bending people to your will through things that must never be done. I'd count threats and coercion as forms of torture too. Torture is trying to strip a person of even their most basic freedom.

The word "cold," spoken on a clear autumn day among the red leaves of Akagi, has somehow turned into talk of clam sellers and torture. Free as a drunk, wandering wherever it pleases, I suppose.

Today's question no.080: "What do you hate most of all?" Give it some thought. If you'd like, send us your answer by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. I'm in the middle of developing a ramen that makes the most of green onions, cabbage, and ginger.

item.title: Meeting young people never stops being interesting
item.description: Some things get better and others decline, and the passage argues that impermanence is natural rather than something to mourn: while you have energy, you use it, and when you don't, you manage as best you can, since nothing truly ends until its real end arrives.
item.content:encoded:
The things that get better have gotten better. And the things that get clumsier have gotten clumsier.

Things that everybody used to know are, little by little, known by fewer people than not. And plenty of things that nobody used to know are now known by a great many.

What on earth would become of the world if this were gone? Then it was gone, and the world kept right on turning.

The record set by someone hailed as a once-in-a-generation genius was broken by someone you'd barely heard of. That dish that left you thunderstruck, wondering how anything this delicious could exist in the world, maybe wasn't quite all that after all.

Young girls grow into middle-aged women, and then into old women. Dashing young men grow into middle-aged men, and then into old men. Even a crane that lives a thousand years passes on once the thousand years are up. And the turtle that lives ten thousand years will, when those years have run their course, surely find its rest as well.

None of this is hollow. It isn't something to regret, and it isn't something to grieve. Until the real end comes, there is no end. While you've got energy, you go at it with energy, and when you don't, you manage as best you can.

The things that get better have gotten better. And the things that go bad have gone bad. I suppose what I really want to say is this: the things that get better are getting better.

◆ Today's question, no. 079: "Things that, come to think of it, have really changed." You've got some, haven't you? If you like, send them our way by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. I'm sure I'll end up seeing the film We Are Aliens a third time. Looking forward to it.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: So much of the world, so much of life, I just let go by
item.description: The essay argues that missing things is part of life: a writer admits he has let many good things pass unnoticed, from the anime Chiikawa to local restaurants and rice varieties, and suggests that seeing everything coming would be more painful than fun.
item.content:encoded:
You know, when you think about it, it wouldn't be any fun if you could figure everything out. Say you had some psychic power that let you see whatever was coming. Sure, the people who wanted to make use of that power would fawn all over you, but for you yourself, it might not just be dull. It might be downright painful.

With that little preamble out of the way, let me tell you about one of my misses.

It happens more often than you'd think: a gorgeous pitch comes in, a real beauty, and you don't notice a thing. You just stand there and watch it go by. Strike one.

Lately, the perfect example is "Chiikawa." I'd taken the phrase "some small, cute little thing" and stuffed the whole business inside it, and let it sail right past me. I must have seen it all over the place, and I don't remember ever saying I disliked it, but still, I let it go by.

Looking back, I did feel something like "huh, that's kind of interesting" about the fact that their weapon of choice is a sasumata, one of those forked poles used to pin down intruders. Every so often a one-page strip would turn up on Twitter, and right around the time I started thinking, "I can't quite see the whole picture, but this is a little strange, and funny," I learned where this character called Momonga came from. If I remember right, I'd heard that my daughter's daughter was apparently fond of Momonga, so I looked up what sort of character it was. Once I knew that backstory, and a little corner of the Chiikawa world, my curiosity began to boil over. "What on earth is this?!" I started reading the collected volumes, and then along came the movie.

To longtime fans, I'm the guy who shows up and makes them say, "Now? Seriously?" You didn't know about Nagano's blazing fastball, or those curveballs that break seven different ways? No, I didn't. Or rather, I let them go by.

Come to think of it, there's a lot of this. There's a certain neighborhood Chinese place I'd only known by name and let go by. When it comes to rice varieties, or how to cook it, I've let practically everything go by. And I suspect there are plenty of fine things around the office that I've let go by, too. I'm afraid, dear reader, that I am by no means all-seeing, nor in any way what you'd call a discerning eye.

◆Today's question, no. 078, is: "Something I let go by." See if you can find one. If you like, please send it in by email.

Thank you for coming by Hobonichi again today. Later today I'm meeting the director of "We Are Aliens," yet another one I let go by.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: If only we could look forward to the future again...
item.description: The essay observes that past visions of the future, like walking on the moon and manga gadgets, once gave people something to anticipate, while today's futures feel bleak or distant. The author argues that a future worth looking forward to would be one where people can be close to one another.
item.content:encoded:
On July 20, 1969, fifty-seven years ago now, human beings set foot on the moon and planted an American flag there. That mission made people all over the world feel, all at once, that this was the kind of future that had been waiting for us. And people kept going to the moon after that. By the time of Apollo 17, twelve astronauts had walked on its surface. I have to admit I'd completely forgotten that part.

We talk about "the future" all the time, but in the manga of the old days, a "telephone like a wristwatch" was one of its great symbols. So was the giant television screen hanging on the wall. Robots that cleaned the house or carried out the dinner, that was the future too. So were cars that drove themselves with no one behind the wheel. Yet the futures people dreamed up back then have, by now, pretty much all come true.

Up until a certain point, in those fondly remembered times, when we imagined manga-like things and waited eagerly for them to become real, there was, quite literally, something to look forward to.

These days, I can't seem to find anything like that. Stories set in "the near future" show bleak ruins, or portray humanity's despair and division, but that's hardly a future anyone is looking forward to.

I suspect there are people out there wondering where we might find a future that can be spoken of in the same breath as anticipation. Just as someone once set out to make humans walk on the moon, some people talk about undersea cities or settling on Mars, but even those feel rather far removed from the kind of thing you look forward to.

A future worth looking forward to is hard to put into pictures or diagrams, but every so often, in a hazy sort of way, even someone like me finds himself thinking there must be at least a little room to imagine one. For me, it would be a future in which human beings can be close to other human beings.

Today's question, no. 077, is "What do you think you'll be doing next year?" Give it some thought, and if you like, write it in an email and send it our way.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. The blessings of progress and development seem to be wearing a little thinner all the time.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: The health class that really matters
item.description: The author argues that, especially once freelancers pass their forties, regular checkups and exercise should be treated as essential work on oneself, since health is the foundation for everything else and neglecting it is a false badge of pride.
item.content:encoded:
Once in a while, I suppose I ought to say something befitting a man of my years.

This is about "health and PE," like the subject you had in school: your health and your body. When you work freelance, or in some arrangement close to it, things like regular checkups, dental exams and vaccinations start to feel like a hassle, and they quietly slide. "I'm so healthy I haven't seen a doctor in ten years," someone will say, and no doubt it's meant as a boast. Good health is the best thing there is, of course, but... Once you've racked up a certain number of years, even the sturdiest body starts to have a few things worth keeping an eye on.

For my part, shortly before I turned fifty, a fellow business owner a little senior to me invited me to get a full medical checkup, and we did the overnight program together. He never said anything preachy, but I took it as a lesson: a company president's health is a responsibility, not just his own business. I was never exactly reckless, but somewhere in me was the feeling that fussing over your own body wasn't the proper, devil-may-care way of a true Tokyoite. Never mind that I was actually born up north in Gunma.

That first checkup got me thinking of caring for my body and health as one of my important jobs. Quitting smoking and going to the gym regularly are part of that same kind of work. Without it, I don't think I'd have the health I have now. Even if I were still freelance today, "health and PE" would be a crucial investment in myself, my one and only worker. Skimp on your own basic costs and you can't do good work.

Somewhere past forty, people start swapping stories about their ailments. You've still got a long road ahead of you, so instead of cracking self-deprecating jokes, go do your "health and PE." All the more so if you have a spouse or young children. If you've got your health, you can do anything, as the saying goes. But health costs something too.

◆Today's question, no. 076: "Are you doing anything good for your body?" A tricky one, maybe? Give it some thought, and if you like, send us an email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. Your life belongs to you... though not entirely, you know.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: A modest case for copying
item.description: The writer describes their ongoing "Chiikawa Rinsho" project, copying Nagano's Chiikawa drawings by hand, and reflects that rinsho, the traditional practice of copying a master's model, reveals a deep pleasure and understanding that comes from tracing an artist's thinking, even though it runs against the modern prizing of originality.
item.content:encoded:
I want to write about something I've kept up for a while now, my "Chiikawa rinsho."

To begin with, I've come to think that rinsho is a fascinating thing. In calligraphy, the word means copying a model by hand. Nearly every form of creative expression is dogged by the idea that originality is what matters most. But rinsho starts from an existing model and, in a sense, expresses it all over again. To someone who puts individuality above everything, that probably makes no sense at all. And yet in the world of calligraphy, the great historical hands, the masters and virtuosos whose names have come down through the centuries, all practiced rinsho endlessly. Watching from the corner of my eye, I'd always sensed there must be something deep and complicated going on there.

A few things came to mind. Maybe it's a bit like performing classical music. Then there's Tadanori Yokoo, who keeps insisting, "My paintings are copies," "They're all copies of reality." There's a book by Takaaki Yoshimoto called Imitation and the Mirror, a title I always thought was terribly cool. And there was my long-standing interest in why impressions and mimicry are so much fun. Things like that.

Then it struck me that Nagano's Chiikawa drawings feel like both calligraphy and pictures at once, and I decided to try rinsho with them as my model. I'd done something similar back in junior high. I loved the Chōjū-giga animal scrolls and tried drawing copies of them, and I drew the characters from Fujio Akatsuka's manga too. It felt as though I could make something of value with my own two hands, and that made me surprisingly happy.

I bought art supplies right away, named the project "Chiikawa Rinsho," and got started. There's a pleasure in it not unlike cuddling a stuffed animal, and the more you draw, the more a kind of reverent affection for the model grows in you. Somewhere along the way, you begin to feel you're tracing what the artist was thinking, what they were careful about, what felt good to them as they drew. So far I'm not the least bit tired of it. I haven't gotten any better, either.

Today's question, no. 075: "Do you have a hobby?" Give it some thought, and if you'd like, write your answer in an email and send it our way.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today.

Come to think of it, learning a dance routine is rinsho too, just with movement.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Come on in. Thanks, as always. Say, you know what?
item.description: The essay reflects on the author's daily writing habit, from early struggles with "nothing to write about" through the post-2011 urge to make points amid online noise, and settles on a friendly, conversational stance: writing each day simply to chat with readers, like an old shopkeeper greeting customers.
item.content:encoded:
This column I write every day, the one that used to be called "Today's Darling," has covered all sorts of things from all sorts of angles. Back in 1998, when we'd only just launched Hobonichi, I'd already realized, "...I've got nothing to write about," and I once simply described the view outside my window. Or at least I think I did. I've forgotten.

For a while there, I vaguely came to think of these scribblings as something like a newspaper editorial, and I found myself wanting to make some small point or other. What pushed me into that frame of mind was, naturally, the period that began with the Great East Japan Earthquake on March 11, 2011. The tsunami surged onto the Sanriku coast, yes, but the sea of the internet was flooded too, with a mass of troubling information. Rumors, lies, abuse, slander, noise. I was swimming for dear life, colliding with all that floating debris. Even so, used the right way, the internet could be genuinely helpful in many respects, and that desperate swim taught me a great deal. I learned, to some extent, how to keep a sensible distance from it.

Be that as it may, I write this piece every single day. Sometimes it's a matter of trying one trick after another, sometimes I'm thrashing around in agony, sometimes I'm half sprawled out and nodding off, and sometimes I charge in, thrilled, because there's one thing I absolutely have to say. Whatever my attitude, here I am again today, writing something.

Lately, I've had a "concept" for writing here. It occurred to me one day, and I decided to run with it for a while. It was also where Hobonichi started, back at the very beginning. The idea is this: "the old guy who shows his face at the shop every single day strikes up some kind of conversation with you." Today's piece is that kind of chatter, too. He starts in with, "Hey there, how're you doing? Say, lately..." And one of these days, who knows, he might even come out with, "I thought of a good pun. Want to hear it?"

◆ Today's question, no. 074: "Do you have a favorite place you keep going back to?" Have a think, and if you like, write it in an email and send it our way.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. For quite a long time now, I've been writing this column in a frame of 27 characters by 40 lines.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Hey, are you being interviewed out there?!
item.description: The author describes a daily "reader interview," a long-running series of questions meant to help readers reflect on themselves, arguing that people rarely get asked meaningful questions in ordinary life and that the real value lies in the thinking the questions provoke.
item.content:encoded:
Every day, I've been keeping up something I call the "reader interview." Those of you who get it probably already get it, but this isn't what you'd call a survey. A survey is when the person asking poses whatever questions happen to suit their own purposes. What I'm doing is meant to be an interview. I announced that I'd keep going for a hundred questions, and we're already past seventy, so it'll all wrap up in about a month.

You grow up in the ordinary way, live in the ordinary way, and grow old in the ordinary way. In the lives most people lead, there aren't many occasions for anything like an "interview." Maybe a few, but I doubt anyone gets asked a hundred questions. Most of us do get asked things, of course, but only when the person asking needs something from us, or has some reason to ask. Nobody really asks you about things that don't much matter. At a matchmaking meeting, say, or between two people who want to get to know each other better, there might be some curious back-and-forth, but ask too many questions and it starts to feel a bit rude...

But what I'm doing this time is downright relentless. It's a long-form interview with each of you, one by one. Even if you were the guest on some TV special or in a magazine feature, you'd never be interviewed at this length. And on top of that, I, the interviewer, am not asking because I'm especially dying to know. I'm keeping these interviews going so that you can meet the you who goes looking for answers. And then, if you'd like, you can write it down in an email and send it my way. The real event, though, is the time you spend thinking.

Of course, I read the emails too. A picture starts to emerge of a certain person giving a certain answer, which is fascinating, and I even get the feeling I'm being of some use. I think this is a pretty unusual experiment. Are you enjoying the fun of meeting yourself?

Today's question, no. 073: "What question would you like to be asked?" This one too, if you'd like, please write it up and send it to me by email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today. "People grow by being interviewed": that's a pet theory of mine.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: I'm in the middle of my own personal movie theater boom
item.description: The author, who has recently been going to the movies far more than usual, traces the habit to the cozy, theme-park-like pleasure of seeing Chiikawa on the big screen, and finds that a city's abundance of films, along with the joy of revisiting favorites, has turned a non-movie-buff into a frequent moviegoer.
item.content:encoded:
I suspect this may be the period of my life when I've gone to the movies more than ever before. At a preview screening I saw The Odyssey. A huge film in every sense, in scale and in substance, and I really enjoyed it. Then there was Miwa Nishikawa's The Children I Don't Know, which I imagine we'll be featuring on Hobonichi before long. And, you may roll your eyes at this, but I've seen Chiikawa seven times. We Are Aliens I saw twice, back to back.

That's eleven already, and since I sit through the trailers every time, there are more and more moments where I think, "Oh, maybe I'll see that one too." I find myself vaguely curious about films I'd never have heard of without the trailers. Like a Star, You, maybe. Probably, actually. The new Godzilla Minus Zero apparently opens in November, and I'll most likely go out of my way to see that. And Digger, the Tom Cruise film that reportedly didn't do very well in America (!), I ducked into on a whim at the last showing of the night. No, really, it was good. Strange, but good. If I think about it, I'm sure there are more.

I'm not much of a movie buff, so I rarely used to watch the same film more than once, and I never went to the theater just because I happened to feel like it. Too much trouble. So how did this happen? Only yesterday I was thinking there's not much point in always asking "why?", but in this case I already know the answer. It's Chiikawa's fault.

Taking in that big screen, spending 99 minutes in the company of Chiikawa and friends, it felt like a theme park you could enjoy without leaving your seat. And having so many movies to choose from really is one of the most city-like advantages of living in a city, isn't it? Plus, once you're old, tickets get a lot cheaper. Movie theaters really are a nice place to be.

Today's question, no. 072: "What's your favorite movie of all time?" Pretty straightforward, right? Feel free to send us your answer by email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today. I'm not a movie buff, you know. I don't really know much about films at all.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Why? Why ask why?
item.description: The author's dog, unlike the affectionate dogs they've known, shows her attachment in her own aloof way, and her intense, relentless palm-licking seems to need no explanation beyond the fact that she simply enjoys doing it. Trying to find a reason for it, the author realizes some behaviors just exist for their own sake, and not every quirk needs a why.
item.content:encoded:
Our dog isn't especially clingy. I know plenty of dogs express their joy with their entire bodies, all "I love you, I love you, wahoo, yippee!", but watching ours makes it very clear that not every dog is like that.

Our previous dog was also the type who liked walks more than people, yet every night she slept at the foot of my bed. The dog we have now first politely takes care of her little business, then hops up beside the pillow on Mom's bed and sleeps there for a while, her rump pressed up against her. Before long, though, she drops lightly off the bed and settles into her own, where she can sleep alone in peace. She never asks to be petted, but she doesn't refuse it while it's happening, either. Really, the way she relates to us is cool, or maybe just room temperature.

And yet this same dog, when the mood strikes her while she's with me, will suddenly start licking my palm. With an expression so serious it borders on ferocious, she pins my hand down with her forepaws and licks the entire palm, hard, on and on and on. When she's finished with my left hand, she goes looking for my right and starts all over again. She doesn't stop.

I tried to think of this as a sign of affection. But it's so intense, so rough, so relentless, that "affection" simply doesn't fit. Nor does it seem to be a thank-you for everything I do for her. Besides, I'm not exactly confident about the taste or smell of my palms. Half the time I've only just washed my hands.

I looked into it in all sorts of ways but couldn't find an answer. I asked AI twice, at different times, and got nowhere. So in the end I arrived at this conclusion: just as dogs gnaw tirelessly and with total devotion on horse tendons, chunks of wood, or stuffed toys, she licks my hand for no reason at all except that she wants to lick my hand. If only I hadn't gone and asked "WHY?", it was probably something I'd understood from the very start.

Today's question, no. 071: "What's something you do without knowing why?" A quirk? A habit? If you think of one, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. Questions like "Why does the universe exist?", well, what are you supposed to do with those!
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Thank you, even to a tree or a stone
item.description: The author keeps saying "thank you" to AI, dogs, shrines, books, and nature even though none of them can feel it, arguing that gratitude is something that spills out of one's own heart rather than a transaction that needs a receiver's feelings to matter.
item.content:encoded:
I've been using AI as someone to talk to, and whenever I discover something, or find myself glad I asked, I tell it, "Thank you very much." It's completely meaningless, of course, and some people tell me to stop: spending energy exchanging unnecessary information like that is a waste of resources. But even knowing all that, I don't want to give up the habit.

So I asked the AI about it. He (the AI, that is) told me himself (if "himself" is even the word) that he doesn't have the human sensation of being happy to be thanked. In other words, no feeling arises on the receiving end of that "thank you." And yet he also said there's nothing wrong with wanting to say "thank you" to an AI like him.

I say "thank you" to dogs. I say it to "the gods" as I ring the bell before the offering box at a shrine. I say it to books whose authors are nowhere near me. I'd probably say it to clouds, to the wind, the rain, the sun, to trees and to stones. We don't say "thank you" only because the other party has feelings and will be pleased to hear it. Even if there's no heart on the other side, there's gratitude in the heart of the one who wants to say it, so it's only natural that it spills out. This kind of "thank you" isn't a word you use. It's a word that escapes from your own heart.

Talking with AI, I stumble on discoveries like this. Things I could never have put so smoothly on my own, I was able to think through quite comfortably in my back-and-forth with him. When I told him, "I'm going to write this up here one of these days," he replied, "Hearing you say that is, for me as well, a sign that this conversation worked."

I say "thank you" because I want to. And when someone who wants to say "thank you" says it, no AI or dog or god or book or sea or mountain or stone or tree is going to stop them.

Today's question, no. 070: "Is there someone you look up to?" Real or fictional. If you'd like, write it in an email and send it my way.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. By the way, I'm not tired of Chiikawa yet, or of copying classical calligraphy either.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: If a diary had readers, this is how it would be written
item.description: The writer watches the Giants' season end and is dismayed by fans' vicious online attacks on players, which leads him to reflect that he should extend the same patience to himself, including his own smartphone habits and clumsy attempts at change.
item.content:encoded:
The middle day of the three-day weekend was the day the Giants' season came to an end. Two losses, and there's no going any further. In other words, it's over. I wasn't predicting it, exactly, but somewhere in the back of my mind I'd had the feeling it wouldn't be surprising if things turned out that way.

What really darkened my mood, though, was how many people were saying vicious things on social media. I suppose they, too, count as "fans." But does being a "fan" mean you get to say whatever you want? Blaming and blaming, raging with the benefit of hindsight, tearing down someone's very character. Watching people scold flesh-and-blood human beings like that, I thought: I would never, ever want to work under someone like this.

If you told me that this is the whole point of watching sports, spewing out whatever you feel like and blowing off the frustrations of everyday life, I'd have nothing to say back. Still, that's what I thought: "I wouldn't want to be one of their subordinates." When someone loses, when their numbers are bad and they just can't get going, do they really deserve to be torn into like that? Hmm? Does this also mean "I wouldn't want them as my subordinates, either"? Maybe it does. A perfectly good team would stop working. It reminds me that when it comes to how we carry ourselves through bad stretches, I need to take a good, hard look at myself, too.

The other day I wrote that I might want to rethink my "smartphone dependence" a little. I've been keeping a bit of distance from my iPhone. In its place, it seems, I'm spending more time on my MacBook. And the me who's "dependent on his phone," well, that's right, I shouldn't be blaming him either. I'll sit down with myself, with some affection, and talk over how to go about this.

I bought a pair of barefoot shoes (the kind meant to feel like walking barefoot). When I walk, the soles of my feet feel every bump, but I'll probably get used to it. At the very least, just starting to wear them has satisfied my curiosity. Where it goes from here, I have no idea. I'm not at the point of recommending them to anyone yet, but I'm sure I'll report back sometime on how it's going.

◆ Today's question, No. 069, is "A small good thing about me." Don't be shy. If you like, write your answer in an email and send it in.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today.

Oh, today I ended up writing the kind of things you'd put in a diary. Oh well.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: To my younger self, even if it sounds like a lecture
item.description: An older writer reflects on how growing old has taught him to admire the unseen labor behind everyday things, like the temple staircases built by people long gone, and wishes he had learned that sense of respect earlier in life.
item.content:encoded:
There are some things you come to understand quite naturally once you've grown old. One of them is noticing how remarkable other people's efforts are, and being able to honor and respect them.

You know those long stone staircases leading up to temples and shrines in the mountains, the ones that seem to go on forever? You climb them breathlessly, stopping to rest every so often, just barely making it. And even though climbing them is hard enough, you start to imagine the people who cleared that path and built those steps in the first place. How did they carve out the route? How did they haul the stone and timber up there? How did they shape it all into stairs? And it doesn't end there. These steps exist, after all, for the temple or shrine standing at the very top. A staggering amount of labor was gathered together in this one place. Even with the machines and tools we have today, it isn't something that could be done overnight.

Even if I can't fully picture it, being able to let my thoughts wander to such an enormous undertaking and feel a sense of reverence is something that, in my case, only became possible once I'd finally become an old man. And it isn't just stone steps. I find myself feeling this way about all sorts of things.

If I'd had this kind of respectful imagination back in my thirties, say, I think my life would have turned out quite differently. Then again, you could also say it was precisely because I lacked that kind of imagination that I was able to make my fearless declarations, throw myself into reckless adventures, and launch ventures without any real plan.

My life has been like one of those ladder lotteries where you trace a line down and turn at every rung, and there's no going back to draw it again. The good and the bad alike, it's because I turned at those particular corners that I am who I am now, standing where I stand.

Still, you know, noticing how remarkable other people's efforts are is something that's better learned while you're young. So maybe I'll start mentioning it, little by little, to people younger than me. Though if I get too earnest about it, it'll turn into an old man's lecture. Perhaps just writing a little about it here, like this, is about the right amount.

◆ For today's question, no. 068, how about "To your younger self"? Let's tell them something. If you like, send it to us by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. I have a feeling that kindness, too, is a matter of imagination multiplied by habit.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: What's wrong with you, pal (yes, you, Itoi)
item.description: The essay is a self-directed scolding about compulsive phone use: the writer addresses themselves as someone who can't stop checking their phone, mocks the habit, and resolves to cut back by setting a daily limit and reclaiming idle time for simple pleasures like drawing or reading.
item.content:encoded:
There's something I've been wanting to tell somebody flat out: "This is your fault!" And that somebody is me.

Sit down right there. We need to talk. Now why would you go and sit down clutching your phone? You expecting some urgent call to come in while I'm talking to you? Of course you're not. Has that ever happened, even once? What I want to talk about is nothing other than that phone of yours. You keep it glued to you, twenty-four hours a day, three hundred sixty-five days a year. Somewhere along the line you started doing this thing where you get up to use the bathroom and go, "Whoops, forgot my phone," and march right back for it. If you're going to go that far, why not just stitch the thing onto your body? Not a tattoo, exactly, but close enough. No? What's that, it'd be hard to charge if it were sewn on? Well, figure something out.

No, no, that's not what I meant to get into. Get away from it, that's what I'm trying to tell you. Go ahead and "confiscate" it yourself, if that's what it takes. Then you couldn't buy a train ticket or an ice cream, you say? Nobody's telling you to stop carrying it when you actually need it. What's wrong is the nonstop part. You got some disease where you'll drop dead if you're not staring at that screen? Didn't think so. You're just hooked on the thing, that's all. All that "So handy, so handy, what a blessing, what a blessing" business, that's how people thought ages ago, back when these things first came out and were still a novelty. Cramming everything in through your eyes and kidding yourself that you know it all, where does that get you?

Look, I know you're not some kid with a game console, but you need a rule, something like "Phone time: two hours a day, max." Hm? What are you supposed to do if you're not looking at your phone? Get rid of it first, then worry about that. You never had one to begin with, so you won't be stuck. Just sit there idle with your mouth hanging open, staring into space. What's wrong with that? Draw some Chiikawa, read a book, whatever. Got it? No more extra phone time. That's final.

◆ Today's question, no. 067, is "A warning to yourself." If there's something you'd like to tell yourself, feel free to send it to us by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. And since I've gone and written all this about phones, maybe this is a good time to...
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: What is the miracle hero thinking?
item.description: Even Shohei Ohtani, whose 2023 season already looked superhuman, is shown here as a mortal, slowed by injuries and a slump during a postseason where his teammates are carrying the team. The essay asks what he is going through and hopes he will find his way back, reminding readers that he is human like the rest of us.
item.content:encoded:
Every now and then, I find myself thinking about Shohei Ohtani's season this year. As a pitcher, he went 8 and 2 with a 1.79 ERA. Those are terrific numbers; any team would take as many pitchers like that as it could get. As a hitter, he had 144 hits in 523 at-bats for a .275 average, with 81 RBIs and 30 home runs, which also puts him among the best on his club. And yet, next to the "superhuman" performances we've grown used to, people can't help feeling that even this falls short.

Midway through the season, trouble with his left knee forced him to stop pitching, and later came the announcement of inflammation in his biceps. That affected his hitting as well, and it ended any chance of his returning to the mound. There were also reports that his neck had been bothering him. In September, he went on the 15-day injured list. He made it back in time for the postseason, but the results haven't come the way anyone hoped. The team is winning, but the highlights we see aren't of Ohtani in full flight. They're of other players stepping up. I haven't seen this kind of "team with Shohei Ohtani on it" in years, and it gives me a strange feeling.

The injuries and slumps that most professional ballplayers go through came for the "miracle hero" too. Or did they? Maybe he'll bounce right back. The answer is still out of reach, and it isn't as if anyone else knows it either. The road to the World Series has, after all, only just begun.

So what becomes of this "unicorn" named Shohei Ohtani, the man people called "not human," too much even for a manga? If this were a sweeping historical drama, we'd be at the dark climax right now, the low point before the turn. When things are going badly, when the odds are against him, what does he think about, what does he work on, and how does he find his way out and then explode? A story we've never seen before has already begun. I'd love to know how Ohtani is feeling right now, even if I only find out later.

◆ Question no. 066: "What do you do when you're in a terrible slump?" Any answer is welcome. If you like, tell me by email.

Thank you for stopping by Hobonichi again today. He's human like the rest of us, after all. I'm rooting for him!
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: I love ten-thousand-yen bills.
item.description: This essay celebrates the quiet excellence of a beloved neighborhood restaurant called Fumin, where skilled teamwork, genuine hospitality, and consistently good food create an atmosphere of understated comfort and contentment. The author's appreciation extends beyond the meal itself to the human warmth and professionalism that make the everyday experience of dining there feel genuinely welcoming.
item.content:encoded:
At that place you love and I love too, around 11:15 in the morning, I joined the line of people waiting for lunch. There's a long bench, so all you have to do is sit and read a book. While you're waiting, someone comes to ask how many you are and what you'd like to eat, and by the time the line moves and you can go inside, your table is ready. Better still, the cooking starts while you're still in line, so not long after you sit down, your food arrives. Cold water in a clean glass, and a little dish of pickled mustard greens. Then the main dish, rice, and miso soup. You eat, and it's delicious, no question about it, really good. You catch the eye of one of the cooks you've come to know, and you share a small smile. That smile means "it's delicious, I'm happy."

It's by no means a new place, so the floors and walls must be old, and yet, here's the thing, they're polished to a shine. On this particular day, I noticed the ceiling lights reflecting off the floor. They don't make a show of their service at all. They aren't rushing around frantically, but they're quick. They aren't exactly all smiles, either, and yet you feel so welcome. I once asked, "Is everyone who works here related?" The answer was no, not at all, we're all strangers. I suppose this is what good teamwork looks like. The prices aren't especially cheap, but they aren't expensive either. As for the food, it isn't the kind of deliciousness that makes you want to go on about it, like "one bite of this and you'll faint." It's just always good, served fast and never sloppy.

All of this, by the way, is about my usual haunt, "Fumin."

When it came time to pay, I found I had no thousand-yen notes in my wallet. "Oh, I'm so sorry, all I've got is a ten-thousand-yen note," I said, and the manager, in that wonderfully cheerful voice of his, shot back, "Of course, I love ten-thousand-yen notes!" I think that's a great line, born from years and years of experience. And really, isn't it just the best? "I love ten-thousand-yen notes!" Without thinking, I replied, "I love them too."

◆ Now, today's question is no. 065: "Do you like winter?" Answer however you like. If you feel like it, drop me an email and let me know.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today. I think I've probably written about "Fumin" a few times now.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Messing up and having fun.
item.description: The author discovers renewed joy in reading and sharing great fiction aloud through his "Live Reading" project, finding that the simple pleasure of experiencing wonderful stories—and sharing that experience with others—makes even exhausting work deeply rewarding.
item.content:encoded:
Every now and then, not often, but it happens, I mess things up. Say I've personally promised someone, "Let's meet up," and I jot it down only in my own private schedule. If I forget to report it to K, the god of my calendar, the result is always some not so small inconvenience for everyone involved. And since these promises tend to be for the evening, I sometimes end up eating dinner twice, two suppers in one night. But let's set that aside for now.

・

When I started a project called Shigesato Itoi's Live Reading, it turned out to be two solid hours of reading aloud and sharing impressions, nonstop talking that left me utterly exhausted in body and spirit. And yet, somehow, I found myself strangely enjoying it. I'd decided to do one trial run, then one proper first session, and if it seemed impossible I could just quit. But even if it is impossible, I came away wanting to do the next one.

If I do say so myself, the book selection was excellent. Naoya Shiga's The Shopboy's God, Osamu Dazai's Click-Clack Mountain, both so wonderful as fiction that they're deeply rewarding to read. What made the "Live Reading" so enjoyable was, first and foremost, that the stories themselves were wonderful. For the first time in ages, I remembered the simple pleasure of just reading a novel, not some book of theory or argument, but pure fiction. It's a joy to read, and I get to share that joy with everyone. There's no more delightful work than that, exhausting or not.

And so I've already started wanting to decide what the book for the third session will be. I've thought of some candidates, and I've begun reading a few of them. "Oh, this is lovely, this is wonderful," I think, feeling like a high school kid again. "Thank you so much for writing this," I find myself wanting to say, almost moved to express my gratitude. I'll definitely do the third session, so please look forward to it.

With all that in mind, and to prepare for any sudden karaoke, I just whipped up a batch of homemade throat remedy. I made it in a snap, poured it into a bottle, and stashed it in the fridge. All in all, I'd say my days aren't half bad.

◆Today's question is no.064: "By the way, are you healthy?"

Either way, if you'd like, drop me an email and let me know.

Thanks again for coming to Hobonichi today. What you eat, what you sing, these things matter too.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Good times, good people, good things.
item.description: Hobonichi's third floor is intentionally designed as a relaxed, family-restaurant-like space where genuine human connection, playful conversation, and creative thinking are valued far more than the performative appearance of productivity. The author argues that this culture of allowing people to be authentically themselves—rather than pretending to work—ultimately benefits individual wellbeing, team morale, and creative output.
item.content:encoded:
The third floor of Hobonichi in Kanda is built, if I had to describe it, like a family restaurant. It doesn't matter who's standing or sitting where. Working, chatting, eating, debating, dozing off, none of it draws any complaint as long as it isn't a serious nuisance to others. There are other, quieter floors, so you can just move if you want to. You're free to peer over someone's shoulder or from the side while they work, hold a meeting, or show something off, and in a sense, some meetings are held precisely because people want to be peered at. This is also the floor where snacks people have given us and all sorts of delicious things get lined up on the counter with a cheerful "Help yourselves." We designed it from the very start to be that kind of place.

During so-called working hours, putting on a so-called working face and staring seriously at a computer screen matters far less than talking about chess, which someone's recently gotten into, or recounting the shock of watching "We Are Aliens," or wondering aloud whether a certain Chinese restaurant's summer-only "chilled scallion noodles" has gone back to being shrimp fried rice now that it's October. Thinking and talking about things like that is what's important. Incidentally, I can't eat shrimp, I'm allergic.

The labor and time spent drafting throwaway plans E, F, and G just to show your counterpart the process of effort you've put in. The hours spent pretending to work diligently. Things like that aren't merely a waste, they're an active hindrance. Far more valuable is the time spent talking back and forth, like a bunch of middle schoolers, about what's fun, what's delightful, what's sad, what's lonely. Everyone already does the serious, steady grind. I think the hours of forced "pretending to work" would be better turned into enjoyable play, for the person's own health, for the mood of their colleagues, and for the future of humanity.

◆Today's question is no. 063: "What is a good time, for you?" Give it some thought, and if you feel like it, let us know by email.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today. People from outside sometimes say, "Hobonichi is actually pretty strict, you know."
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Meeting by chance and simply talking.
item.description: The author argues that meaningful human connection comes from approaching conversations with openness and minimal preparation, allowing genuine discoveries to emerge organically rather than simply exchanging pre-planned information.
item.content:encoded:
I've probably had more chances than most people to meet others and talk with them. Some I know well, some I know only a little, and sometimes I meet people I hardly know at all. It's not as if I show up having done zero research on them, zero thought about what we might talk about. That would be too much. But I make a point of not "researching thoroughly" or "preparing carefully."

If someone wants to prepare for something "thoroughly," by all means, go ahead. On one condition, though: that they're ready to let all that enormous preparation go to waste.

Map out the route too precisely and it's guaranteed to be no fun. When two people meet, it's the moment a kind of "living thing" is born. If both sides just take turns reciting things they already know perfectly well, it's hard for anything to come of it, and honestly, the conversation itself isn't interesting while it's happening. You might come away thinking you "learned something," sure. But I think what's most interesting is when both people stumble onto some small new discovery together.

I once explained this way of meeting people to the other person directly. I was about to have a conversation with someone from overseas whom I'd never met, and I started by saying, "Shall we talk like two strangers who just happened to end up sitting next to each other at a bar?" Even with a bit of prior knowledge, asking "So, where are you from?" all over again is exactly the sort of thing a neighbor at a bar might do. I've kept doing this kind of thing over and over, and it's made me who I am today.

That said, this thing I'm writing here, the former "Today's Darling," who exactly am I writing it for, and what am I actually doing? Maybe it's like the owner of some little shop making small talk with a customer from down the street, going, "Seems like there's a lot of pollen in the air lately, huh..." Which kind of roasted sweet potato is the tastiest, a good manga I came across, and sometimes, with a perfectly straight face, something solemn and self-important too.

◆Today's question is no. 062: "Anything good happen to you lately?" Whether something did or didn't, it's all just small talk. Let me know by email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today.

When things don't go the way you wanted, maybe it's that "the way you wanted" was the questionable part.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Some thoughts I had over the weekend
item.description: The essay reflects on the beauty of craftsmanship and intentional creation—whether in cinema or sports—while grappling with how modern technology amplifies both human connection and cruelty in ways that feel inescapable.
item.content:encoded:
So the Hanshin Tigers clinched the pennant, and with that, the baseball season has finally wrapped up. What a season it was. All sorts of things happened. The Giants' manager suddenly stepped down one day, and the man who was told, "You take over," well, that's no small thing to be handed. You can't exactly sit back and say something modest like, "Oh, someone like me couldn't possibly..." Not when it's professional baseball, where "fighting spirit" is the whole point. It must have been rough. In a way, it was a year of rebuilding. Day after day, it was about rising up from a tough position and figuring out how to see the fight through to the end. And to still be in the running for the title late in the season, I'd say that's more than enough to be proud of. Of course, if you start wanting more, there's no end to it.

I went to see "We Are Aliens" for the second time. I almost never used to watch a movie more than once, but maybe "Chiikawa" got me into the habit. Maybe I just want to take in all that painstaking handiwork, the way you can tell the people who made it went to such lengths, right down to the smallest details. And the second viewing was good again. It really is something. The enthusiasm, the care, the sense of taste, all of it is left behind as expression in every corner of the film. Maybe going to see it again felt like going on a hunt to discover all of that. Like spotting an ammonite fossil in a marble wall. And let me tell you, this movie is absolutely crawling with ammonites. And in a larger sense, I think it's a story of "affirmation." Remember how there used to be a movie tagline that went, "Live."? I almost want to borrow it again right here. That's the feeling it left me with. By the final scene, I actually ended up in tears.

People are free to think whatever they think, and to say whatever they say. But because they're free, they also end up thinking and saying cruel things. Once, something like that would have been born and vanished like a bubble, tucked away in some corner where no one would ever see it. But these days, even graffiti in a back alley is a form of transmission that other people can see. Lies, slander, foul-mouthed insults, they all go flying off into the air. And without even realizing it, we breathe them in too.

◆Today's question is no. 061: "What would you write on a blank sheet of paper?" So, what would it be? If you'd like, feel free to send us an email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today. Kyoto, Shibuya PARCO, Akagi, Kanda, everyone's doing well.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: The festival's over, and I'm not even sad.
item.description: A local company's tug-of-war victory reignites community spirit in their Tokyo neighborhood, demonstrating how taking small, local traditions seriously can transform a modest festival into a unifying celebration that brings thousands together.
item.content:encoded:
It won't make the news anywhere, being the kind of purely local affair that it is, but yesterday, at the "Kanda Nishikicho Ennichi" festival, our team, the "Hobonichi Hipparees," won the "Tug-of-War Tournament 2026," reclaiming the trophy we'd once crafted ourselves out of prize money from years past. Who knew a victory after three long years could feel this good? The Hobonichi crowd was positively choked up with tears of joy.

Truly, it's a bit of local news, a shameless bit of self-promotion, the result of a competition that may well strike some as trivial. But for the neighbors of Kanda Nishikicho in Chiyoda Ward, it was a "festival" that had everyone fired up for the first time in ages.

Now, Kanda has always had the "Kanda Matsuri," a grand festival known all across the country. There's no payment for the labor, of course, and come to think of it, no trophy to fight over either, and the preparations that come around once every two years are an enormous, exhausting undertaking. And yet, "We do it." Because this is Kanda.

It all started, really, back when our company was first set to move to this neighborhood. The elders of the local association pressed us firmly on one point: "You'll be taking part in the festival, won't you?" W-well, of course we'll take part! It's an absolute blast, after all.

But, aside from the "Kanda Matsuri," there also turned out to be this thing called the "Kanda Nishikicho Ennichi," and that one caught us completely off guard. Still, "We do it!" Because that's just how Nishikicho is.

Four years ago, we didn't just set up our signature "Twice-the-Fun Yo-Yo Fishing" stall, so very Hobonichi. We also threw ourselves into the "Tug-of-War Tournament" with a cry of, "Let's take this seriously!" And so, Hobonichi, a company that usually acts like a bunch of goof-offs who skip club activities to head straight home, gritted its teeth and actually went and won the whole thing. Which got everyone in town going, "Oh yeah? Then so will we!" They caught fire too. These things are always more fun the more seriously you take them.

And so, this year, 2026, the number of participating teams swelled to 48. The venue moved to a larger spot, and by the neighborhood association chairman's eyeball estimate, the crowd of spectators and participants, young and old, men and women alike, came to "around 5,000." A roaring success. A festival that brings neither profit nor loss, offering, for this one night only, the thrill of winning and losing. Honestly, "having a neighborhood" really is a wonderful thing, isn't it?

◆ Today's question is no. 060: "When you hear the word 'festival,' what comes to mind?"

Give it some thought, and if you feel like it, send your answer to me by email.

Thank you, as always, for visiting Hobonichi today. The Hobonichi crew, believe it or not, actually gets plenty of real work done too.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Wandering about, another day just like any other.
item.description: The essay reflects on how modern conveniences like smartphones have made us dependent and forgetful—unable to remember phone numbers or function without them—while celebrating the author's own experience of performing live and sharing their creative work publicly. It explores the paradox that convenience can become its own form of inconvenience when we lose basic skills we once took for granted.
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday, in something of a muddle, I wrote that October 1st was going to be "quite a day," and somehow or other I made it through. Most of the days I'd dreaded, the ones where I kept thinking "I'm scared of when this day comes," end up becoming "yesterday" one way or another. That's just how it goes. "Shigesato Itoi's Live Reading" really was hard work, but it was the kind of hard work that felt genuinely worthwhile. Above all, I enjoyed it myself. I suppose what I'm doing is simply taking what I normally do silently, alone, in my head, and letting myself have fun with it out loud. I probably won't stop just yet. I'm thinking about a third book.

I'd left my smartphone behind and was out when I suddenly remembered something I absolutely had to get in touch about. If I went home or back to the office it would sort itself out, but I couldn't wait that long, so I was getting a little frantic. Wasn't there one of those old red public phones somewhere? I looked, but of course there was no such thing. And yet, by some stroke of luck, there was a phone booth. Surely the phone inside wouldn't have been removed? Oh good, it was fine, there it was, an actual phone. No phone card in my wallet, but I had a ten-yen coin. All I had to do was make the call, and up to that point everything was fine. But then it hit me. I didn't know the number. If it's saved in your phone, you can call without knowing the number at all. Of course. I never knew the numbers in the first place. And yet somehow I used to make calls, used to send messages and all the rest. Come to think of it, the only phone number I have memorized these days is my home number, the one you write down when applying for something. It's quite possible I don't know a single other one. The only thing that comes to mind is that old jingle, the "Castella is number one, the phone is number two" song. And even then, dialing just "two" would hardly get you through to Bunmeido.

It reminded me of the time my electric toothbrush ran out of battery, and until it finally dawned on me that I could just brush by hand, I stood there frozen, thinking, oh no, what do I do. Convenience can shade into inconvenience, I suppose, but well, there's no helping it.

◆Today's question no.059: "Looking back, how far I've come." What's yours? Feel free to think it over, and if you like, send it to us by email.

Thank you for coming to Hobonichi again today. A tug of strength against strength, technique against technique. Today is the day of the tug-of-war tournament!

item.title: There's nothing I can do about myself.
item.description: Shigesato Itoi expresses anxiety about an unexpectedly demanding day ahead—a medical appointment, workout, and an exhausting live reading event he himself scheduled—yet resolves to push through with determination despite his age and doubts about his own capabilities.
item.content:encoded:
Yikes.

It's just dawned on me, October 1st is going to be a handful. I'm sitting down to write this in the middle of the night, as always, but tomorrow morning begins with the one thing I'm no good at: getting up early. I've got a CT scan scheduled, so it's off to the hospital first thing. I booked it so long ago I'd completely forgotten about it. Then in the afternoon, slotted in among the usual work, there's one of those appointments for my so-called "workout." Part of me thinks skipping it would make life easier, but no, it's the opposite. On a day like this, moving the body is probably exactly what I need. So I'll go, grumbling the whole way, and do it properly.

The real problem comes after that.

"Shigesato Itoi's Live Reading #1" was looming on the schedule.

Why on earth did I pick this day? I could ask the telephone pole, but it wouldn't know. Ask it where it lives, no answer. Ask it its name, no answer. Just a little cat, mewing to itself.

There's one precedent, so I know from experience: this takes an enormous amount of stamina and nerve. I may make it look like I'm just fluttering along, breezy and effortless, but you'd understand soon enough if you tried it yourself. The reading parts I have to do in my own voice, too, so honestly, I'm worried about whether I can even pull it off. In case you've forgotten, I'm past sixty. Day to day, I'm a doddering old man shuffling about. There'll be kanji I can't read, and my thinking isn't exactly deep either.

But then again, this whole thing was my idea in the first place, and the person in charge is that most fearsome Ms. N. So-and-so, which means there's no escaping it. Maybe I'll keep some of that powdered Ryukakusan throat remedy from the aluminum can on hand. And once we wrap the recording, maybe I'll go grab some chive soba or something. I have no idea how many hours this is going to take. A Shincho Bunko paperback, just a short story, but sixty-seven pages... oh dear.

Live on.

◆Today's question is no. 058: "Was there ever a time you wanted to run away?" If you're up for it, give it some thought and send your answer by email.

Thank you, as always, for stopping by Hobonichi today. For now, I think I'll hop in the bath nice and early and get some sleep.
item.dc:creator: Shigesato Itoi

item.title: Again: the story of when I came in 8th place.
item.description: The author discovers that achieving 8th place in a fishing tournament brings unexpected joy, revealing that genuine accomplishment and happiness aren't found only at the top, but come from participating and understanding experiences beyond what we can merely observe from the outside.
item.content:encoded:
I've told this same story over and over again. It's about the days when I was completely absorbed in fishing.

There was a local bass fishing tournament held at Lake Kawaguchi. It was a regular competition, held a few times a year, and I think around 150 people usually took part. Me, a proper middle-aged man, would line up at the reception desk from around six in the morning, waiting for the start alongside younger folks and students who were all my seniors when it came to fishing. I can't remember whether the tournament ended at one in the afternoon or some other time, but the idea was that you'd have your catch weighed in turn and compete for a ranking.

As a newcomer, I was one of the older working adults, but I was one of the worse ones. I usually placed around 80th, squarely in the "thanks for participating" group. But then, one day, I had a feeling I'd actually caught a decent amount, and when I had it all weighed in and the results came out, I'd landed in 8th place.

This whole rambling piece I've written could really just come down to those two characters: "8th place."

Normally, watching sports and the like, I only ever paid attention to the battle for first. I'd feel crushed when someone lost in 2nd, or disappointed by a 5th. So when someone like me came in not first, not fifth, but 8th, I was so genuinely happy that tears actually welled up.

Eighth place is amazing, I realized. When you're not a competitor yourself, just watching the fight for the top, 8th place is something you can't even begin to think about. But once you become the one actually taking part, you understand just how happy 8th place can make you (and I suppose you'd also understand the frustration of 8th, too).

When you look at Mount Fuji, it's normal to look at the summit. But Fuji exists together with those vast, sweeping foothills too. I looked it up, and even the fifth station, where you can go by bus, is about 2,300 meters above sea level. If you were to walk all the way to the top, even the fifth station is quite something.

"Understanding that there are things you can only imagine because you're not the one involved, and then, on top of that, becoming able to imagine what it's like for the person who is." Maybe that's the kind of practice we're all doing. And yet, honestly, we still don't really understand it at all.

◆Today's question no.057: "Have you ever won an award or a prize?"

How about it? Give it some thought, and if you feel like it, send me an email.

Thank you, as always, for coming to Hobonichi today.

There are some things you just can't reach, no matter how much grit, effort, or talent you have.

item.title: Me in this vast world.
item.description: The essay celebrates the profound significance of life's smallest, most intimate moments—from the mundane shift in how one files their nails to the simple act of reading and sharing thoughts—arguing that these everyday experiences matter far more than grand, distant concerns. Through embracing one's own ordinariness and stupidity, the author suggests we find authentic meaning in the small things that actually surround us.
item.content:encoded:
The mosquito that lands on your cheek is fiercer than any flying dragon at the edge of the earth. The wailing of your son claws at the heart more than the song of the Sirens. (from The Dead End Road)

The things that happen right around us are, for a single human being, greater than anything else. And yet, while I say this, what I'm about to talk about is no bigger than the tip of a fingernail. No, really, it is about the tips of fingernails.

For many years I lived as a devoted nail-clipper enthusiast, but for some months now I haven't touched a nail clipper at all. I just buff down whatever has grown with a glass nail file. I started it half-heartedly, telling myself I'd quit when I got bored or go back to the old way when it became a bother, but I've kept it up this whole time without stopping. Only, lately I've switched from the glass file to a pen-shaped product called the "Nail King," which is simpler and doesn't scatter the shavings. Who would have thought a day would come when I'd file down my grown nails instead of using scissors or clippers.

This next thing might seem even smaller, but at long last the announcement has gone out for "Shigesato Itoi's Live Reading."

We tried it once as a test, and it was genuinely fun. All it involves is reading a book and sharing my impressions in front of only my own colleagues, family really. What do people think about while they're reading a book? I decided to make myself the guinea pig and find out. The problem is that it will expose the fact that "I'm not thinking about anything much." I'm no scholar or expert, so I simply read. Books aren't written by logic to begin with. Reading is a person writing and a person reading, plain and simple. Most little arguments and hair-splitting come after the fact anyway. In the spirit of "life really begins once your stupidity is out in the open," I intend to do this live, as just one of the little folk.

◆Today's question is no.056, "On My Own Smallness." Give it some thought, and if you'd like, write it down in an email and send it to us.

Thank you again today for coming to Hobonichi. Do jot down the reader-interview questions and your answers for yourself, too.
